But who is least prepared? 

Today’s over-55s are already rather too aware of their pension choices thanks to frenzied speculation about tax raids in the run-up to the autumn Budget. 

The upshot? Those who have managed to save for retirement are taking it out again in droves. This risks making a bad situation worse for Generation X, the cohort aged 45 to 60, many of whom face a substantial pensions shortfall.

transcript: The US government just shut down. Wall Street normally shrugs off shutdowns, but things could be different this week. With the government closed, we won't get Friday's crucial labor market report, and that's a problem because the Fed wants clean labor market data. It's also coming at a time where the labor market is showing signs of cracking. The stoppage also complicates CPI data collection for the inflation report that's due in just around two weeks. And there's one new variable this time, the Trump administration's promise to commit mass firings of federal workers if the deal is not reached. Details are scarce so far when it comes to how deep any permanent firings and cuts could go, but it does add a new layer of uncertainty for investors and workers alike. Historically, shutdowns aren't big market movers. We've had around 20 plus since the nineteen seventies, and they usually last around a week. Stocks tend to wobble and then refocus on earnings, the Fed, growth, and 2025 has been pretty dang resilient already with tech leading the way higher, a strong September, and the continued hope for further Fed easing. So what could markets do? In the near term, it's more about uncertainty than fundamentals. If the shutdown is brief, history says investors can look through it. If it drags on, the risk is that the Fed flies blind and has to delay cuts or maybe pivot later.

transcript: Are we in a market bubble? Well, it depends on who you ask. At the moment, AI is the hot trade. The stocks have surged, and some valuations look a bit stretched. A bubble happens when prices rise way above what something is actually worth. That's fueled by hype, speculation, maybe even a little bit of FOMO. Everyone piles in until reality hits and the bubble bursts. Think the .com boom. Huge gains, little earnings, and a big old crash that followed. But there are reasons that people think this rally still has legs. One, many companies are posting solid earnings or upbeat guidance that suggests that valuations are fairly valued. The market's also seen more breadth, meaning that it's not just those big tech names leading markets higher. Plus, macro tailwinds like the start of Federal Reserve easing along with cooling inflation in certain categories are giving stocks yet another boost. But strategists are also watching a few red flags. Some say the AI fueled rally may be running ahead of the earnings to back it up. And certain profitless tech names are soaring anyway. That's classic promise over actual ability to deliver. And even with broader participation, the rally is still concentrated with just a handful of mega cap tech companies doing the bulk of the heavy lifting. Bottom line, there may be more upside ahead, but bubbles are always worth paying attention to because no one likes it when one suddenly pops.

transcript: What goes into determining your mortgage rate? The answer might be more complicated than you think. Mortgage rates closely follow the bond market, especially ten year treasury yields. Those yields move for all sorts of reasons, usually based on expectations about the economy and inflation. When the economy looks shaky, bond yields usually fall, and that can make mortgage rates fall too. On the flip side, when there's really good economic data, bond yields usually rise, and then mortgage rates rise as well. So weirdly, what's bad for the economy is usually good for mortgage rates. The ten year yield is about 4.2% right now, but mortgage rates are close to 6.5%. The difference in those two numbers is what's called the spread. Spreads can move for a lot of different reasons, including how much a lender is trying to profit on your loan, how much it costs to originate the loan, and also how much Wall Street is demanding mortgage backed securities right now. But part of what goes into your spread does depend on your personal finances. Factors like having a higher credit score or making a larger down payment will generally lower your mortgage rate because your lender will consider you lower risk. One thing to remember is that the mortgage rates that you see reported are usually only available to the very highest quality borrowers. These are the people with credit scores in the high seven hundreds or above that are putting at least 20% down. So your own mortgage rate may be a little higher, and you can blame the spread.

caption:
The past two decades of French and British politics are a graveyard of proposals to slow the upward ratchet of spending on growing elderly populations. The same two decades of French and British fiscal balances show the results. Public disbursements to older citizens have climbed higher and faster than in peer countries, and debt-to-GDP ratios have followed suit.⁠
⁠
In the UK, the problems are twofold. First is the trashing of both major parties’ attempts to move some of the eye-watering costs of elderly care on to those most able to afford it. Britain’s health and care bill for over-65s has doubled since the turn of the millennium, and without commensurate increases in revenue is both squeezing out spending on infrastructure and increasing borrowing.⁠
⁠
Second is the ‘triple lock’ on the state pension, which guarantees that payments rise each year by whatever is the highest out of inflation, wage growth or 2.5% — an extraordinary deal which guarantees that pension spending growth outpaces pensioner population growth, and ensures elderly living standards increase at a faster rate than everyone else’s. ⁠
⁠
Tap the link in our bio to read the full story. ⁠

transcript: Britain's data is broken. When we think about the big divides in modern politics, two issues stand out, immigration and inequality. Immigration sits at the heart of cultural debates. Inequality defines the economic ones. Together, these questions shape elections, policies, and the very direction of societies. But there's a problem. In Britain today, we don't have the data we need to answer either of them. In recent years, Britain's statistical foundations have begun to crumble. In 02/2023, the Office for National Statistics delayed labor market figures because the numbers couldn't be relied upon. Soon after that, the core labor force survey, the only real source for judging whether immigrants are more or less likely to work than native born citizens, lost its official accreditation. Even basic population breakdowns by nationality were stripped to their gold standard status. The consequences are serious. Without trusted numbers, the debate over immigration becomes a fog of war. Politicians, think tanks, and partisans fill the void with our often in incomplete bias statistics. On inequality, things are much better. The UK's wealth and asset survey, the main tool for measuring wealth gaps, was also downgraded, leaving policymakers guessing as they consider wealth taxes. And it's not just immigration or inequality. From crime victimization surveys to key health metrics, 79 official data sets have been cancelled or decertified since 02/1025 in the past year alone. Not through malice, but through falling survey response rates and official mismanagement. But the effect is the same, less clarity, more distrust. This vacuum hands ammunition to populists. Figures like Nigel Farage can point to the gaps and cast doubts on the entire system. The US faces a similar challenge for different reasons with political interference in official statistics creating fertile ground for misinformation. Good data isn't necessarily about proving one side right and the other wrong. It's the bedrock of informed policy and democratic debate. Without it, Britain sails blind in dark waters with the lights of reliable statistics flickering out one by one.

While attention has been focused on Gaza, Israel has undermined the delicate architecture of governance in the West Bank built up over three decades.⁠
⁠
Earlier this year, Israel sent tanks into Jenin refugee camp in the northern West Bank, and it encountered barely any resistance at all.⁠
⁠
So weakened were the poorly equipped fighters of the so-called Jenin Battalion from intermittent Israeli raids — and also from a weeks-long confrontation with their own government’s security forces — that they just ‘ran away’, says Rayad Hassan, a Palestinian police officer injured in 2002 and displaced in 2025.⁠
⁠
The resistance and the camp’s nearly 25,000 Palestinian residents are gone, forced out by the Israelis and displaced around the occupied West Bank, living in tents, schools and half-completed apartment blocks.⁠
⁠
Nine months after Israeli soldiers entered the camp, they are so completely in control of an area once considered the factory of Palestinian militancy that on a recent afternoon they could be seen driving around in soft-top SUVs, laughing and joking as their bulldozers chomped away at the ruins of the camp.⁠
⁠
The fate of the West Bank will come into focus next week at the UN General Assembly where the UK, France, Canada and Australia — all allies of Israel — intend to recognise a Palestinian state, as do many others.⁠
⁠

caption:
AI generated content is becoming more mainstream, and it’s embedding itself in the influencer market too.⁠
⁠
The proliferation of AI-generated content — and wholly AI accounts — is a central pillar of the strategy of Silicon Valley social media platforms, according to executives.⁠
⁠
For brands, there is the promise of cheap, instant influencer marketing and full control over what an avatar looks like and says.⁠
⁠
But the shift has left some human influencers — particularly those who do not wish to use AI as part of their content creation processes — and their teams fearing displacement or disintermediation. ‘It’s dangerous for artists,’ said creator and plus-size model Gabriella Halikas.⁠
⁠
Some maintain AI will not fully replace the human influencer role as it cannot be related to, an assertion that appears borne out by data. ⁠
⁠
‘AI cannot experience things. It cannot be a tired parent. It cannot have a skin condition, it cannot taste food,’ said Jago Sherman, head of strategy at The Goat Agency, the influencer subsidiary of WPP. ⁠
⁠
He predicted there would be an ‘uptick in influencer fraud’, whereby creators would be commissioned to produce real content but might use AI as a shortcut. ‘If we pay for human content and receive non-human content in return, that’s fool's gold.’⁠
⁠
What do you think?⁠

Political economist, Lawrence Gunther, identifies what he calls a representation gap between the values and preferences of voters and the politicians who've been in charge for recent decades. On economic issues like taxation and public spending, voters and mainstream politicians have long been broadly aligned. But on socio cultural issues like immigration and criminal justice, there's a yawning gulf. Western publics consistently want greater emphasis on order, control, and cultural integration. Their politicians have tilted in the opposite direction, favoring more inclusive and permissive approaches. The result, a wide open space on the political map with large numbers of voters, but few mainstream politicians willing to represent them. The populist right is now rapidly expanding into that space. This pattern is visible across most of the West. In The US, the average voters preferences on immigration sit closer to Republican politicians than to Democratic party elites. When the center left Danish Social Democrats took a tough position on asylum and integration in 02/2019, Voters believed and trusted them, and the radical right threat was neutralized. But it's crucial to understand what voters actually want here. Decades of data show public concern tracks irregular migration and failed integration, not people coming to work and study. transcript: What's in a name? Well, if you take a name like mine, Sarah, there's really quite a lot of history there. So Sarah has had a very much of a rollercoaster time in terms of popularity over the last couple of centuries. In the nineteenth century, people chose from a small number of very traditional names. Sarah was one of them. But the most popular were John and Mary. Something like eight to 9% of all babies were called John or Mary in about the mid nineteenth century. Obviously, since then, things were changed a lot. But sometimes, these old fashion names come back into fashion. And that's what happened roughly around the time that I was born. Sarah suddenly revived in popularity, which is why you probably know a lot of people called Sarah. And as indeed do I. In fact, at one point here at the Feet in the office, part of the office where I sat, we realized there were more people called Sarah than there were men. But what is beginning to happen now is that some of those old fashion names are coming back into fashion again. But there needs to have been a long break between when they were last popular. So people who have babies now, they're looking for something that has some heritage, but they don't want a name that reminds them of their parents' generation or indeed of their grandparents' generation. So that's why people are looking even further back and they're choosing names for babies now like Evelyn or Ada or Iris. But the other big trend is that no names now are as popular as the very popular names of the past. So, you know, the most popular names now will only probably have sort of maybe 2% of babies called that. That's because we're more individualistic today. Everyone wants to be different. Everyone wants to find a new variation on a name spelling. And thanks to globalization and social media, we're exposed to so many more names to choose from. So in the future, I don't think there will ever be a situation again where someone like me is growing up surrounded by people with the same name as them.

transcript: The International Monetary Fund is a body designed to foster sustainable economic progress across the world. With Donald Trump's tariffs, economic ties are facing threats we've not seen in generations. With a 191 member countries, the IMF was set up in 1944 to be the guardian of a new era of global economic cooperation. The fund has two main tools at its disposal. It lends to countries that have run out of money with conditions attached. Borrowers only get access to the funds if they change economic policies, and they have to repay the fund first. The second tool is monitoring and advice. The IMF sends its teams of experts into countries to report on their economies. Of course, they're free to ignore any advice because no money is attached. Without sounding too cynical, the recommendations are often exactly what a country's politicians know are needed, but don't dare to propose domestically. It can help to get a nudge from the IMF. Inside the Fund, voting power is determined by an arcane and out of date formula, supposed to reflect the shape of the global economy. And The US is dominant, holding 16 and a half percent of the votes, making it the only country with a veto on decisions. If the fund's internal power genuinely reflected the global economy, China's voting share would be larger than that of The US. But China's voting share is actually smaller than that of Japan, and only a bit bigger than that of Germany. To date, the IMF is not immediately in the crosshairs of the Trump administration, and it's important to understand why. The fund is mostly self financing, making profits from lending, so it's not coming with a begging bowl to the US government. The biggest borrower by far is Argentina, and its president, Javier Mele, is a Trump ally. All of a sudden, there's also a vacancy for the IMF's first deputy managing director, who'll be an American and appointed by Trump. A trade policy settlement among the main players is essential. And the IMF has rapidly shifted its views to suit the Trump administration, pulling its punches on tariffs and downplaying the importance of the green agenda. The IMF is therefore bending over backwards not to fall out with the Trump administration. But that raises two awkward questions. First, what rescue role can the IMF play if a country has an economic crisis and it's not a friend of The US? And second, if the IMF is mostly focused on saving its own skin by buttering up the Trump administration, how can it still be a relevant force in the global economy?

transcript: Why should progressives care about falling birth rates? Birth rates are falling among progressives but not conservatives. Falling birth rates are rarely out of the news these days. Births hit record lows in The UK, US and much of Europe last year. But what those headlines miss is that the decline isn't spread evenly. It's disproportionately people on the progressive left who are having fewer children. Progressives place a higher value on women's freedom to choose and many worry that population growth could worsen the climate crisis. In this sense, having fewer kids and bristling at birth rates discourse more generally is the natural progressive position. But beneath the surface, there's a paradox at play. Let's start with the politics. If people on the left have fewer kids, the demographic balance tilts right over time. Sure, many children rebel against their parents' politics, but on average there's still a strong correlation between the politics of parents and their kids. Indeed, studies find that a drop in the number of children raised in progressive households has already pushed US and European politics to the right. Falling birth rates on the left also means shrinking workforces and growing elderly populations which require increases in tax rates and immigration to support, both of which can spark conservative backlash. What about the environment? Many assume fewer people equals lower emissions but reality is more complex. Carbon emissions are driven much less by the number of people emitting than by how much each one emits. Emissions in the West have fallen rapidly even as populations have grown thanks to cleaner technologies. This matters because younger societies are more innovative while older ones often resist change. So the decline in progressive birth rates can actually slow further progress in tackling climate change rather than helping the planet. Ultimately, whether or not to have kids is a deeply personal choice. But if people are choosing childlessness because they believe it's greener or more progressive, the evidence suggests they should think again.

The streets of Kathmandu are marked by the signs of revolution.⁠
But it is an inscription with black marker on a marbled wall of the charred parliament building set on fire in Nepal’s capital last week that encapsulates the moment: ‘From now, only Gen Z youth will be in this place. Corrupt leaders will be sent out of the country. Long Live Nepal. Long Live Gen Z youth.’⁠
⁠
The demonstrations in Nepal have been called the protest of ‘Gen Z’ — which generally refers to people born between 1997 and 2012 — after young people, some in school uniforms, took to the streets against what they saw as an ageing and crooked political elite.⁠
⁠
However, it is just the latest in the region. Amid a dire economic crisis in Sri Lanka in 2022, tens of thousands of protesters, mainly youngsters, converged on Colombo, the commercial capital, and over-ran the presidential palace. Then president Gotabaya Rajapaksa, now aged 76, fled the country on a military aircraft for the Maldives.⁠
⁠
In Bangladesh two years later, students from Dhaka University led an enormous popular uprising that eventually forced the country’s authoritarian ruler, 77-year-old Sheikh Hasina, to flee to India. Indonesia briefly looked like it might be next last month.⁠
⁠
Which country in Asia will be the next domino to fall?⁠

transcript: Rural Spain is emptying out, so the Spanish government is getting creative. Sparsely populated regions are so common that they've earned their own nickname: Espana Mafia or Empty Spain. While 84% of Spain's territory is rural, only 16% of people live outside cities. People have been living for years, driven by a lack of jobs, poor infrastructure, and almost no cultural offerings. Spain's rural areas saw a 4.4% population decline between 2014 and 2023, even as the country's overall population grew. To confront the problem, the government has started rolling out grants, tax breaks, and incentives to make moving back to the countryside more appealing. At the same time, new real estate agencies are popping up, helping urbanized parts of city life find cheaper, quieter homes in the countryside. Some investors are going even bigger, buying entire villages, restoring them and turning them into venues for weddings or retreats. Private organizations like Alma Natura are helping entrepreneurs settle in the populated towns, despite challenges such as poor internet and distance schools. Critics say government measures are too little, too late, but people's renewed interest in life outside cities could turn the tide and save a few small towns.
